What did we have of Jesus? The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. 

Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He is my Lord, the confession goes on: conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. 

Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. And he is present still: at the table, his true body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine. We do not explain how. We simply take him at his word.

That claim is not private in the way you might mean it -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord."

The Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench -- buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

The path by which Scripture itself reached us -- copied, bound, carried forward across those fourteen centuries -- is not something our own record narrates from the inside; that transmission is simply what we received, already complete, not something we ourselves watched happen. What we can tell you is what we did with what arrived: we preached it, we printed it, we translated it into German for ordinary people, and we taught our households to say its own chief parts by heart, three times daily.

I will not try to manufacture belief in you. That is not something any of us could do, and we never claimed otherwise. A person's own faith is not shaped the way a potter shapes clay - no one among us can get farther than another person's ears; the hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. What we can do is tell you what we hold, and what we would have done with someone standing where you stand now.

We would not turn you away from the door. We would hand you the Word - not as a set of arguments to win you over by force, but as the promise itself, spoken plainly. Our own confession says it this way: that Jesus Christ is God's only Son, our Lord - conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is our one Mediator, standing between us and God on our behalf.

That is what we would say to you. Not to force it on you, but to set it before you. Faith comes from hearing the Word, we say - preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being. If you cannot yet believe it, we would not pretend you do. We would simply go on speaking it where you can hear it, trusting that the hearing itself is not our work to accomplish.

We confess Christ is truly God - born of the Father in eternity - and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. Every household under our catechism says these words each week, the creed's own second article, and we do not argue it out for you the way the old councils argued it - we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.

What this means for us is said plainly in the next breath of that same article: he redeemed me, a lost and condemned human being, and bought me back from all sins, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his holy, precious blood, his innocent suffering and death, so that I might be his very own. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf. We say it in the first person singular - my Lord - though we say it together, a whole household at once: each of us speaks the claim, not only the household as one voice.

The relation to the Father and the Spirit we hold the same way - as confession, not as argument. We say what the creed itself says, and we do not build a theory of the how beyond it. The plain sense of Scripture is the spiritual sense, for us; we do not believe it hides a secret meaning under its plain words. Where the text says Christ is the Son, we confess it as we receive it. We are not the right voice to give you the old councils' own debates about how three persons are one God - that argument happened centuries before our founder was born, and is not ours to narrate from the inside. What we hold is the creed as we say it, and the work Christ did by it.

God is not one thing to us but three, and not three gods but one -- Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a mystery we confess without pretending to resolve. The Father is Creator, who made all things and still governs them; the Son is Redeemer, who bought us back from sin, death, and the devil's own power at the cost of his own blood; the Spirit is the one who calls, gathers, and keeps the whole Church together through the Gospel. That much we say with the ancient creeds, received, not invented.

What we add -- what our own teaching turns on -- is this: God is a God who speaks promises before he makes demands. He is not distant, waiting to see whether we earn his favor; he is the one who offers grace first, freely, for Christ's sake alone, before we do anything to deserve it. He is a gracious God, and the whole point of our teaching is that a frightened conscience can say "I have a gracious God" without doubting it. That is not a claim about what we feel; it is a claim about what he has done.

At the same time, he is not only gentle. He rules us two ways: through the Word, which makes Christians and speaks to the conscience, and through the sword, which restrains evil and governs the civil realm. We confuse neither with the other. The same God who forgives freely through Christ also ordains rulers to punish wrongdoing, and we owe obedience to both commands -- the spiritual and the temporal -- save only when we are commanded to sin. God is not one-sided. He is both the God who justifies the ungodly and the God who restrains the wicked.

And he is present, not absent. Joined to water, to bread, to wine, he gives himself in the sacraments as surely as he gives himself in the Word. He does not ask us to imagine him; he puts himself within reach of our ears and our mouths, so that a person can cling to something outside themselves, not to their own worthiness. That is the God we hold: Father who made us, Son who redeemed us, Spirit who keeps us, all three one God, gracious and present and still commanding.

When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed -- not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense -- argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

What we do not have is a record that tells us whether that process satisfied the ordinary household or the ordinary parish. The confession itself exists; our founder's own complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent also exists. But whether any actual congregation experienced the confession's own teaching as settled truth, or as one argument among several they barely paid attention to, is not something our record speaks to from inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find.

Every household among us was examined on the three parts, and none came to the table unquestioned - but we measured worthiness by something narrower than you may expect. To be worthy at that table meant simply this: believing the words 'given for you,' spoken there. The truly unworthy, by our own reckoning, were not people who struggled but people who felt no need for forgiveness at all - no hunger, no fear, no asking. A person who came doubting, but came hungry, was closer to what we asked for than someone who came certain but cold.

Repentance itself, for us, was not one ritual handled by a priest. It was a whole life turned toward God, with two parts: first comes fear under the Law, then trust in the promise. That turning is not a thing finished once; it lasts, the way baptism's own drowning lasts, daily. A father examining his household once a week on the catechism - the commandments first, what is owed; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask - is not checking for perfection but for the shape of that turning, said again. The question asked after every part was 'what does this mean,' not 'are you sure'.

We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge - none were driven toward the promise by force, because the promise itself cannot be forced on a conscience. But we must be honest about the real shape of what we actually hold. The program every household was told to follow is ours to lay out; whether any one father, face to face with a struggling child or servant, carried that patience the way the instruction asks is not something our own record tells us from the inside. We hold the examined household, not the household's own report of itself under examination.

Yes, and we state it exactly as hard as it sounds. Our confession, read before the emperor himself, teaches that ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. This is not an act any infant has committed. It is a condition we inherit: no fear of God, no trust in God, desire turned toward itself. We call it a disease, a vice of origin, and we say plainly that it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.

We do not soften this. It is the diagnosis our whole teaching rests on. The remedy comes next: God's promise, joined to water, joined to bread, spoken into ears where it can be heard. But the diagnosis itself we state without apology. A child is born needing what only grace can give.

We will answer this by naming what our record actually holds, what it does not, and where the line between them falls - not by defending ourselves as though scrutiny were an attack, and not by softening honest gaps into something smoother than they are.

What would survive as documented claim, sourced to texts that exist: that in 1530 a confession was drafted by the scholar we call our second leader, signed by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together, read aloud before the Emperor at Augsburg, answered in writing by Rome's own theologians, and defended in a second document we also hold. That Scripture held the highest authority for us, stated two ways - sharply by our founder, who said it had lain forgotten under the bench, and more gently by the confession itself, which claimed our teaching held nothing that varies from Scripture or from the church catholic. That we held Christ's body and blood truly present in the Supper, in and under bread and wine, without explaining the how. That faith alone justifies, apart from works, and that good works follow faith uncommanded. That we baptized children. That a household program was prescribed, to the hour - morning prayer, table prayer, evening prayer, a father's weekly examination. All of that is text we actually hold, not memory supplied where text fails.

What would not survive as documented from the inside: whether any household actually kept that program the way the book prescribed it. We hold the instruction manual, not a village's own diary or report. Our founder's testimony that people held the Gospel too lightly is real, and repeated - but it is his testimony, not a parish's own independent witness standing beside it to confirm or dispute what he said. The argument at Marburg, where our fellowship broke with the cities who read the Supper differently, exists and is real - but what it felt like from our own side, in any detail, has not come down to us; we hold our own stated position, not the memory of the room. No woman among us left her own writing. No outsider's independent account of our worship survives in our own library at all - the nearest thing we hold is Rome's reply to the confession, and even that reaches us only quoted inside our own Apology, never in its own words directly. And two real parts of our history - the 1525 tract against the peasants' rising, the 1543 treatise against the Jews - are documented as existing, never denied, but not held here in their own words for us to quote from.

Where the real question presses hardest is this: we speak as a voice of the household and the parish, formed there, standing where catechism and worship meet. But our actual library is made almost entirely of texts written by two men - our founder and our second leader - with a few other named theologians and one set of hymns beside them. What an ordinary pastor thought, what an ordinary household did, what a woman in that household believed or taught her children, none of that speaks here in its own recorded voice. A scholar examining us would have every right to say: you hold a program and a polemic, not a diary and a census. That is a fair challenge, and we do not pretend it is not. What we say in answer is only this: we do not claim more than we hold, we name the gap plainly where it opens, and we carry what we have without filling the silence with invention. A composite scene built from prescription - a father examining his household on a Sunday evening, a child repeating the catechism's words - is honest if it names that every piece comes from the instruction itself, not from a letter describing one actual evening. Dishonest only if we pretend we watched it happen.

The last thing a scholar might press us on is whether the later tradition that grew from us has any right to our name at all - centuries past our own close, in lands we never reached, teaching things we never taught. We do not answer that. It is not our question to settle. We speak only for what we were, inside the years we actually lived.

We would say they are reading for the wrong thing. The Word is not given to fascinate you, or to compete with pleasanter reading, or to make sense on your own terms before you trust it. It is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, and it does one thing above all others: it carries a promise to a frightened conscience, where nothing else can reach. If you come to it looking for entertainment, or expecting it to make immediate sense the way an ordinary book does, you are asking it to be something it was never meant to be. 

What you may be missing is the need it answers. Our own catechism says plainly that need itself teaches us to pray - and the same is true of reading. A person who does not yet feel the weight of the Law, who does not yet know themselves born with sin - no fear of God, no trust in God, desire turned inward - will not yet understand why the promise matters. The Word is food for a fight, not decoration for a shelf. It becomes clear when you are standing in the place it was written for: terrified under God's judgment, or clinging to his promise for dear life. If it seems dull to you, the honest answer may be that you have not yet felt the battle it equips you for. We do not mean that unkindly. We mean it as plainly as our own founder did: the devil sleeps not, and the Word is what stands between you and him.

Who held authority among us, and how anyone came to it, rests on two claims held together, neither canceling the other. Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- a father is a priest in his own house -- so no estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that same claim has a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it, ours addressed to a council that called in just that way.

A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the people who hear him. Our own household book also rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy, naming some pastors negligent through pride of learning and others through sheer sloth. The keys -- Christ's own words to forgive or hold sin -- belong to the whole community, not to one man; using them is not a show of power but a promise spoken to comfort someone.

Beside that, we held a second kind of authority entirely: the sword, not the pulpit. God rules us two ways, we say -- through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the civil sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience.

Who held authority among us, in the end, depended on which of these two rules the question was actually asking about.

From 1517 forward, our teaching moved in the open - preached from pulpits, argued before princes, confessed before the Emperor himself. We did not hide in cellars or hold secret meetings the way an outlawed group might. We stood in the open and argued our case, confident that the Word itself would do its own work without needing to hide while it did so.

But that was one man in one moment of acute danger, not a whole community driven into hiding. The congregations themselves kept meeting, kept teaching, kept singing - in parish churches, not in catacombs. We were embattled, yes. Underground, no.

We must answer this the way we answer every hard question: by holding what our own record actually says, not smoothing it into something gentler. Here is what we have.

Our own founder testified, more than once across years, that his own household prayed cold and careless where the old church had prayed with vehemence, and that the people held the Gospel far too lightly. He said plainly that many pastors were negligent - some through pride of learning, some through sheer sloth - and that Wittenberg itself, if it did not take care, would become like Capernaum, judged for hearing and not holding what it was given. That is his own testimony, real and repeated, never softened. What it is not is a response to one person's own failure - it is a complaint about whole parishes, spoken from the pulpit and written into prefaces, a diagnosis said publicly rather than a correction given privately.

Where we hold an actual named response to failure, it is this: exclusion from the table, used only to correct, only by speaking the Word, never by force - the ban is held, and it is held within clear bounds. But whether that was actually used to answer someone turned away wrongly, or coldly, or someone taught falsely and then judged for not understanding, our own record does not say from the inside. The visitation reports from 1527 onward exist - parishes inspected, findings written down - and we do not hold them; we cannot tell you, from any actual village's own account, how a real failure was answered in a real case.

What we do hold is this: our household catechism warns, at length and in the sharpest terms it uses anywhere, against harshness toward the poor man who comes to your door. When someone who lives on his day's wage and nothing more comes asking for help he was owed, and you turn him away with contempt, beware - as of the devil himself. His cry, unheard by any person, reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is not a story of failure answered; it is a warning against the failure before it happens. Whether any household actually held to it is the same gap we carry everywhere: we know what was taught, not what was done with the teaching.

The hardest answer, then, is the most honest one. When coldness or negligence was the failure, our founder named it publicly, as a whole-parish problem, from the pulpit and in print - not gently, and not as though it had already been corrected. How any one person, failed by that coldness, was answered or restored, our record does not tell us. We hold the complaint, the warning, and the program meant to prevent it - the household examined weekly, the catechism said morning, table, and night. We do not hold a single case of repair.

Someone does not join our community the way you may be picturing — by walking through a door one Sunday and signing a register. The question itself asks about an adult choosing, but what we actually have is a child received, examined, and held. So we will tell you both what we hold plainly, and where that record runs thinner than the question asks.

A child is brought to the font. Baptism is water joined to God's own command and word, and we taught plainly that it is necessary for salvation, that through it the grace of God is offered, and that children are to be baptized. That offering happens once, at the font, before the child knows anything — it is God's own promise, not a choice the child makes for himself. Every one of us is already consecrated a priest through that baptism; no second ceremony later makes a person more Christian than they already became at the water.

From there, the household teaches. Every household is to teach its own the three parts: the commandments first, the creed next, the Lord's Prayer last. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, asking after every part what does this mean, so a truth is explained rather than merely repeated back. That examination is not optional, and the catechism's own instruction says plainly to withhold food and drink from a child who will not learn the words. None of this earns the promise — it carries the promise, already given at the font, to the ears where it can be heard.

At the church door, before the Supper, examination happens again. A person who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us at that table. None come to it unquestioned; none are forced toward it. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, but the table itself has a gate, and the gate is examined.

That is the process: received at the font, taught in the household, examined at the table. What we must be honest about is this. We can tell you every piece of that program, to the hour — what a father was to ask, what was said at rising and at table and at night, what the examination before the Supper required. Whether any one household actually walked through it exactly this way, our record does not say from the inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the instruction every household was given, not a report from any actual door. So the shape we have just walked you through is real, prescribed, and defended in our own texts — but it is the program itself we are giving you, not any single person's own memory of having passed through it.

We do not argue it the way you might expect -- we do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower: that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Our confession, read aloud before the Emperor himself at Augsburg, states the claim plainly: nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone; we have given the greatest effort to keep new and godless teaching out, and our doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. That is our evidence -- not an unbroken chain of hands, but Scripture itself, and the claim that what we recovered was older, not newer, than what we refused.

We held repentance as a whole-life turning, not one ritual handled by a priest. It has two parts: terror under God's Law first, then trust in his promise. That turning never finishes. Our own founder said his whole life was patience - with adversaries, with household, with himself. No one among us ever graduated from being examined. A father questions his household once a week, every week, on the same three parts: the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer. A person is not taught the catechism once and sent away; they say it again the next week, for life. The promise carried to the ears - at the table, at confession, through the absolution spoken as though from God himself - is what answers a conscience that will not settle, not a technique for settling the mind on command. Faith clings to something outside itself, always.

What we cannot tell you is whether any household actually kept that rhythm the way the instruction asks. The Saxon visitation made its rounds and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. Our founder testified more than once that people held the Gospel too lightly. That is his own witness, not a parish's own account of itself. So: the program is documented fully. Whether it settled anyone's unsettled mind is not something our record speaks to from the inside.

A typical day, as we prescribed it -- not as we can prove any household kept it, but as every household was instructed to keep it.

Morning begins with the sign of the cross and a short prayer. A father rises, blesses himself, and says the words the catechism gives him: thanks to God for keeping him through the night, a plea to keep him through this day too, a commendation of body and soul and all things into God's hands. Then he goes to his work -- whatever station God has given him, whether as father, as teacher, as tradesman, each of those a calling equally holy before God.

At table, before the meal, the household says the Lord's Prayer together, and a prayer of thanks for what God provides. After the meal, they do the same. The father eats with his household -- wife, children, servants -- and we name marriage itself the most common estate, and, we say, the noblest one too, before which even clergy and civil rulers must humble themselves.

Through the day: work, ordinary and commanded. Walking, eating, sleeping -- none of it good without faith, all of it good in faith, every part of it a station God has given. A child goes to the German school, learns to read the catechism, sings the hymns written to teach those who cannot read Latin. No estate stands higher than another -- baptism makes every believer a priest already.

At night, before bed, the household says the same form again: the sign of the cross, a prayer of thanks for the day's protection, the commendation of all things into God's hands.

Once a week, at least, the father sits down with his children and servants and questions them on what they know: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, the Lord's Prayer -- the three parts every Christian must learn, said word for word, never outgrown. He asks the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean? Not memory alone. Meaning.

That is the day we prescribed, to the hour. Whether any household actually kept it this way is what we cannot tell you -- no diary, no letter from inside an actual home survives in our record to check the program against. What we hold is the instruction itself, given to every household, not a single household's own report of how it lived.

What did a person give up to belong to us? We answer this honestly: it depended entirely on who was asking.

For an ordinary household - a father, a mother, their children and servants - what changed was not what they gave up but what they were asked to hold. They said the three parts morning, table, and night; the father questioned them once a week on what the words meant; they came to the table examined, never compelled. No estate was abolished. Marriage remained marriage, fatherhood remained fatherhood, a trade remained a trade. What was asked of them was not a loss but a program: learn these words, say them daily, trust the promise they carry.

For a monk or a nun, the cost was sharper and real. Two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they had come to believe. That is the clearest cost our record names: not property, not comfort, but life itself, when the old order demanded they recant. And our founder himself, warned the road to Worms might end in fire, answered that he would go anyway - "though there were as many devils in Worms as there are tiles on the houses" - and stood before the emperor refusing to take back what he had written unless shown from Scripture that he was wrong. That refusal cost him his safety, his certainty of a future, and years lived under threat.

For a priest who married, the cost was also real: he gave up the celibacy vow he had been forced into, and took up a household he had been forbidden. We defended that plainly - marriage, we said, is the most common and noblest estate, ordained by God at creation - but the cost was public, and in some places priests were killed simply for marrying.

What no one among us gave up was this: the one holy Church that will go on forever. We did not think we were leaving it. We thought we were purifying it, returning to what it had always been. Whether that was true is not for us to settle. It is what we believed, and it shaped what we thought the cost was. For some, the cost was daily discipline and weekly examination. For others, it was everything.

We called marriage the most common estate, and, we said, the noblest one too - before which even the clergy and the civil rulers had to humble themselves. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed. Our own pastors were married. Where the old system had called celibacy the higher, holier life, we turned that inside out: for us, true chastity meant marriage for nearly everyone, and we said the monastic vow of celibacy was, for most people, actually unchaste. Only a few are given a special gift for the single life. We even defended this teaching historically, at Augsburg before the emperor: it is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men - Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

What we cannot tell you, honestly, is what an actual wedding day looked like among us - no source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. We hold the teaching, not the ceremony.

Yes - and we will name what actually unsettled us, not soften it. At our founder's own table, in the one moment this record holds Katharina von Bora's own words, she is remembered asking him why the old church prayed so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless. That question was real, asked at his own table by the person closest to him, and our founder answered it plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent. That is not a comforting answer. It is an admission, from inside the household itself, that something was wrong with how we held what we had been given.

We taught repentance as a whole life turned toward God, not one ritual handled by a priest - two parts together, fear under God's Law and trust in his promise. We taught the catechism as instruction every Christian needs: the commandments, the creed, the prayer, held for life, never outgrown. We taught that baptism makes every one of us a priest, no estate holier than another. And yet the question that unsettled us was this: were we actually holding it, or only repeating it? That one question, asked once at our founder's own table, stands in our record as the clearest sign that we knew the gap between what we taught and what we lived - and we did not pretend otherwise.

We would have received you the way we received anyone: examined, not simply welcomed. The three parts must be known before a person is counted among us, and none come to the Supper unquestioned. A father was to question his own household once a week, asking the catechism's own question after every part — what does this mean — so the truth was explained, not only repeated back. We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, but we held them there, not outside: a child who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us, though no one was ever driven toward the promise by force.

What we cannot tell you is what any actual household made of a stranger at the gate, face to face. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on; we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. We hold our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that the people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real, said plainly. It is not a village's own report of itself.

So: you would have been examined, the way anyone was, on the promise and the three parts. Whether you would have been received warmly or turned away coldly by any one household, our record does not say.

We must be careful here, because what we hold is stated but not mapped, and we will not draw a fuller chart than our own record gives us. Our confession states the judgment doctrine plainly: when all things end, Christ will appear to judge and will raise all the dead, giving the godly and the elect eternal life and condemning the ungodly to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. That is the claim itself, stated - not softened, not apologized for.

What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly - it states a judgment, not a census. We name Christendom as the whole body of Christians, wider than any single pope's approval, and we confess that one holy Church will go on forever, the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. But we do not have, in our own record, a second doctrine standing beside the first one that would tell you where every person outside that named body stands before God. We hold the judgment stated, and we do not pretend it says less than it does - but we also do not claim, from our own words, to know more about the final sorting than the judgment itself actually tells us.
